statement: In four people who died in Finland in 2000 and 2001 (aged 18 to 23; one woman and three men), MDMA and moclobemide, a reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant that had not been prescribed to any of them, were both found in post-mortem blood, and forensic pathologists certified each death as combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs (Vuori et al., 2003, a case series with no comparison group). The authors read the sparse histories (sudden confusion, convulsions or collapse; a body temperature of 43.2 °C in the one person whose temperature is given) as consistent with serotonin syndrome, but no sign that defines it (clonus, reflexes, muscle tone, tremor) was recorded in any of the four. Blood MDMA was 1.6 to 2.1 mg/L, 4.6 to 6.0 times the top of the reference range the paper quotes (editors' calculation), and moclobemide 2.1 to 7.9 mg/L, near the top of its quoted reference range in two people (the authors call this the maximum therapeutic concentration) and 2.6 to 3.2 times the top of it in two (a moderate overdose, they say; editors' calculation). Other substances were found in the blood or urine of all four (alcohol, amphetamines, cannabis and, in one man, dextromethorphan at many times the quoted range, which the pathologist counted as a contributor), and the paper does not say whether MDMA alone at these levels could have caused the deaths. Amounts taken are unknown for three; for the fourth, aged 19, the paper states ten tablets without giving a source, and his MDMA level was similar to the others'; the paper says it is not known why the four combined the drugs. As described in narrative reviews, MDMA with an MAOI is placed at the highest level of risk among the combinations with MDMA that they rank (Silins et al., 2007, who cite these four deaths and two older case reports of MDMA with phenelzine, not read here); MAOIs are said to be strongly associated with severe cases when combined with MDMA (Boyer and Shannon, 2005); and one reviewer says that several unpublished cases are known to him (Gillman, 2005). No source read counts the people who took MDMA with an MAOI and had no such outcome, and cases are selected by death, so no rate or relative risk can be given; Silins et al. also state that only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-related serotonin syndrome have been published since the late 1980s. In a technical report summarized by Silins et al., about 1 in 25 people in an Australian study of people who use ecstasy said they had deliberately combined it with moclobemide; the review gives no sample size. People can feel little from an amount of MDMA for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, a medicine that blunts the effect) and some take more; no source read measured what happens then with an MAOI.
plain: Four young people in Finland died in 2000 and 2001 with MDMA and moclobemide in their blood. Moclobemide is an antidepressant that stops the body breaking down serotonin, and none of the four had been prescribed it. Pathologists called each death an accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the authors thought the signs fitted serotonin syndrome, but no examination signs were recorded. All four had MDMA levels about 5 to 6 times the top of the range the paper quotes, and all had other drugs in their blood or urine, so MDMA alone cannot be ruled out. Reviews place MDMA with this kind of antidepressant at the highest risk of the mixes they rank, but nobody has counted how many people took both and had no such outcome, so no rate can be given. Some people feel little from an amount of MDMA, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ, and some then take more; no study measured what happens then with this antidepressant. The evidence is four deaths and reviews.
population: Four people who died in Finland in 2000 and 2001 (a woman aged 18 and men aged 23, 18 and 19), identified by the authors' forensic medicine departments as appearing to be a fatal interaction of MDMA and moclobemide; moclobemide had not been prescribed to any of them. Further cases and the ranking of the combination are described second-hand in narrative reviews.
exposure: MDMA together with the reversible MAO-A inhibitor moclobemide, found in post-mortem blood (MDMA 1.6, 2.0, 1.7 and 2.1 mg/L; moclobemide 2.3, 2.1, 7.9 and 6.5 mg/L); amounts and timing taken are not known (study condition only: one man was reported to have taken ten ecstasy tablets, source not stated); other MAOIs such as phenelzine appear only as described in reviews
comparator: No comparison group: the paper describes no deaths with MDMA alone, moclobemide alone or other combinations, and nobody who took the combination and survived is counted
outcome: Death, certified by forensic pathologists as combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide; the authors' reading of the sparse histories (sudden confusion, convulsions, collapse; one temperature of 43.2 °C) as consistent with serotonin syndrome
magnitude: No rate or relative risk can be derived: four deaths selected by outcome, no denominator. Post-mortem blood (mg/L), MDMA then moclobemide: case 1 (woman, 18) 1.6 and 2.3; case 2 (man, 23) 2.0 and 2.1; case 3 (man, 18) 1.7 and 7.9; case 4 (man, 19) 2.1 and 6.5. Reference ranges quoted in the paper: MDMA 0.1 to 0.35, moclobemide 1.5 to 2.5. Editors' calculation: MDMA 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of its range; moclobemide 0.9, 0.8, 3.2 and 2.6 times the upper end of its range. Body temperature 43.2 °C in case 3 (when it was taken is not stated); none recorded for the others. As summarized by Silins et al. (2007): approximately 1 in 25 people in a recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide (a technical report by two of the review's authors; no sample size, recruitment method or time frame given).

evidence.extracted: The abstract describes four deaths following ingestion of moclobemide and MDMA, says the probable cause of death in each was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs, and infers a purpose for taking moclobemide because none of the four had been prescribed it. The pathologists' stated cause in each case, in the case descriptions, is combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the Discussion says it is not known why the victims combined the substances.

evidence.locator: Method (reference ranges; the single paragraph begins on p. 365); Case 1, Case 2, Case 3 (p. 366); Case 4 (begins at the foot of p. 366)
evidence.extracted: Reference ranges quoted in the Method: MDMA in blood 0.1–0.35 mg/l; moclobemide 1.5–2.5 mg/l. Case 1: woman aged 18, unknown quantity of street ecstasy, next morning suddenly confused, convulsed, lost consciousness and stopped breathing; no temperature taken; blood MDMA 1.6 mg/l, moclobemide 2.3 mg/l; alcohol in blood and urine; amphetamines in urine. Case 2: man aged 23 found dead after a confused state, with two kinds of white tablets that both contained MDMA; blood MDMA 2.0 mg/l, moclobemide 2.1 mg/l, dextromethorphan 1.1 mg/l (quoted range 0.01–0.04), plus morphine, amphetamine, cyclizine and several benzodiazepines; the pathologist counted dextromethorphan as contributing. Case 3: man aged 18 who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years, suddenly confused, rolled about on the floor, collapsed; body temperature of the deceased 43.2 C; blood MDMA 1.7 mg/l, amphetamine 0.15 mg/l, moclobemide 7.9 mg/l, cannabis in blood and alcohol in urine. Case 4: man aged 19 who had taken 10 ecstasy tablets, unconscious with breathing difficulties, died in hospital; no temperature; blood MDMA 2.1 mg/l, moclobemide 6.5 mg/l, cannabis, MDA and lidocaine. In all four the pathologist concluded combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide. No clonus, reflexes, tone or tremor is recorded for any. Editors' calculation: the four MDMA concentrations are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the quoted MDMA range (0.35 mg/l); moclobemide 0.9, 0.8, 3.2 and 2.6 times the upper end of its range (2.5 mg/l).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; paragraph beginning Moclobemide had not been prescribed; paragraph beginning It is not known why the victims combined these substances; last paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors say that, to their knowledge, no fatal cases of this combination had been reported before; that history and clinical observations were limited in most cases, but the mode of death in each was consistent with a serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it; that moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the victims and was present at maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and in moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4; that it is not known why the victims combined the substances; that the only known link between the cases is the region, with cases 1 and 2 close in time; that in case 2 moclobemide could also have slowed the breakdown of dextromethorphan; and that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAO inhibitor, is taken together with MDMA, a statement given without a rate or a comparison.

evidence.locator: Results › High risk, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 651, right-hand column; the 2nd paragraph ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 652)
evidence.extracted: The review places ecstasy taken with MAOI antidepressants (phenelzine, tranylcypromine), other MAOIs and the reversible inhibitor moclobemide in the high-risk group, as likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin. It says cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy with phenelzine have been reported as early as 1987 (two older case reports, not read here) and that ecstasy with moclobemide can give rise to fatalities, a handful of cases being documented (the Finnish series read here); it says further evidence that moclobemide increases the likelihood of severe serotonin syndrome with ecstasy comes from animal studies.

evidence.locator: Results › High risk, paragraph beginning In a recent Australian study (left-hand column)
evidence.extracted: Approximately one in 25 people in a recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide (a technical report by two of the review's authors; the review gives no sample size, recruitment method or time frame); the same research is said to have found that deliberately taking antidepressants with ecstasy went with a greater likelihood of reporting muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and profuse sweating.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (begins in the left-hand column and ends in the right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say that since the late 1980s only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-induced harm that fit the diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome have been described; that the incidence of ecstasy-related fatalities seems low compared with the likely frequency of use, but the extent of acute non-fatal harm is harder to estimate because less serious cases are not usually published; and that fatalities from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy overdose alone are relatively rare, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater when ecstasy is taken together with other serotonergic drugs or substances.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 435 and ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 436)
evidence.extracted: The review states that illicit stimulants such as MDMA, if combined with MAOIs (including moclobemide), also cause fatalities because they act as serotonin releasers; that serotonin releasers with MAOIs are the only other combination, besides MAOIs with serotonin reuptake inhibitors, able to cause serotonin toxicity of a severe and potentially fatal degree; that several unpublished cases of MAOI and releaser combinations are known to the author; and that a recent case series of four deaths has been reported by Vuori (the paper read here).

evidence.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs and drug combinations
evidence.extracted: The review says that MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are strongly associated with severe cases of the syndrome, especially when used in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA, and cites other papers for this sentence; the Finnish series is not among the review's references.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall very high on the study card: no comparison group, other substances in every person, MDMA alone at 4.6 to 6.0 times the quoted reference range cannot be excluded, the cause of death is a judgment by authors who selected the cases, and no examination sign that defines serotonin syndrome was recorded.

inconsistency.note: Not assessable: one case series; the reviews cite it and add no counted cases.

indirectness.note: The primary report concerns one MAOI, moclobemide, a reversible inhibitor of MAO-A; the extension to other MAOIs and to older and unpublished cases is second-hand through narrative reviews that were not appraised.

imprecision.note: No rate or interval is claimed; the lack of a denominator is counted under risk of bias.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; unreported cases are unknown.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the evidence is descriptive or consists of reports, and the rating is already at the floor (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Observational reports start low (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -2 (ROBINS-E very high on the card), indirectness -1 (one MAOI read in a primary report, the rest second-hand through reviews); inconsistency, imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low (the floor). Status single study: one case series read in full; reviews that cite it do not count as further studies. Stays draft: the claim rests on one case series and on reviews (METHODS 6 and 12; brief). The relation is worded as an association in four selected deaths: that the combination caused them is not shown, because MDMA alone at these levels cannot be excluded and the clinical signs that define the syndrome were not recorded. The claim gives no rate, because none can be derived, and no instruction.

verification.flag_note: Kept draft: rests on one case series and on reviews (METHODS 6 and 12; brief). Deliberately not stated: the reasons given for combining MDMA with moclobemide (the Vuori abstract infers a purpose, its Discussion says the reason is not known, and Silins et al. report what survey participants said), because that edges toward potentiation guidance; the editor may decide whether to add it. Not read: Smilkstein 1987 and Kaskey 1992 (phenelzine with MDMA, cited by Silins), Parrott 2002, Demirkiran 1996 and Gillman 1997 (cited by Boyer), the Copeland et al. technical report (2004) and survey (2006; Reader 51 holds it second-hand), and Gillman's unpublished cases. The Silins statement that susceptibility can last up to 2 weeks after stopping a long-acting MAOI could not be traced in Gillman and is not used. Overlap: Reader 51's claims on antidepressants with MDMA leave MAOI evidence to this claim; the Buckley et al. remark that serotonin-releasing drugs might attenuate an SSRI's toxicity concerns an SSRI taken with a releasing drug and is not used here.
